chapter: Sarah Vaughan and the Basie band
title: Basie band discipline on the Birdland bus tour
summary: The Basie band sounded fresh after long bus rides near Butte, Montana, and Jones considers how Basie and Ellington hold bands together.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: And I've been -- I've experienced that thing, especially with the Basie band. I think the other day I was speaking about when we were doing one nighters on the bus, and we'd gotten near Butte, Montana someplace. This was the Birdland show. And the guys had sat up so long, their feet began to swell. Of course we got to a hotel later. But the Basie band went on the stand and they sounded as though they'd had 48 hours sleep.
They always could really click, you know? And as quiet as Basie is, he doesn't seem to be a disciplinarian, but he gets the discipline.
Is it -- do you think it comes off of Basie, or is it -- what is the spark? Is Basie the spark in that band that gets it together?

Oh, I have to see. Well, I have to give it to Basie, because he had the first band. He's had five or six or seven different bands. But he gets about -- the common denominator is the same. As with Ellington. Still get that -- those two guys had a knack, you know. Basie still has it. They had a knack of getting some -- the musical thing out of the men, and to hold it together. Every time they -- oh, of course, Pat, as you know, there were different levels. Sometimes the guys would get tired, being on the road. But there was no bad music. It was good, better and best.

What do you think makes the difference? Is there any way to analyze what makes the difference between a fantastically good night and an acceptable performance? Because it's not just weariness. We know, and like you just said --
